extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, playwrights, and educated readers interested in dramatic criticism and the qualities of tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for evaluating a stage tragedy (character, plot, moral effect, language, and stagecraft), illustrated by a detailed critique of the play Bertram. Focuses on dramatic probability, moral purpose, diction/metre, and practical staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: union of desirable human qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The character (e.g., Don John) should consist in 'the union of everything desirable to human nature' and be displayed in its own dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters gain life from a combination of attractive traits—manners, wit, gaiety, and social generosity—that can make even a criminal interesting without reducing him to a mere ruffian. Example: Don John's gentlemanly manners suffuse the drama with life. Avoid flat villainy; complex mixture of qualities is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and balance of dramatic ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients of a play should be 'mixed in the happiest proportion, so as to uphold and relieve each other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a constant interpoise (e.g., of wit, gaiety, and generosity) so that tonal extremes do not overwhelm the piece; balance prevents characters from appearing one-dimensional and keeps scenes from collapsing into mere spectacle or mere ranting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic probability and causal coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every event and scene must have credible causes and effects and fit into the natural order of things; dramatic surprise should be prepared, not arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing effects that lack antecedent causes or consequences. Anti-pattern: a prodigy or miracle appearing 'without any circumstance mentioned that is prodigious' and 'ending without a result.' If an event could as well have been mundane (e.g., a common gale), its supernatural framing is gratuitous and weakens probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural effects must be prepared and grounded
rubrics_metrics.description: A supernatural prodigy should be signalled, justified, and produce consequences; not a 'miracle introduced without a ground, and ending without a result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the audience: establish antecedent conditions, motives, or symbolic logic that make the supernatural intelligible. Do not use ghosts/portents merely for startling spectacle; they must advance plot or theme and have discernible effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose and demonstrable ethical value
rubrics_metrics.description: A play should be 'susceptible of a sound moral'—its incidents and portraiture ought to demonstrate ethical truths or warn against hollow accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the drama shows why certain traits or social shows are hollow or dangerous (rather than merely displaying them). Avoid presenting gentlemanly qualities as substitutes for virtue; the moral aim should be clear and persuasive rather than merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of character should not excuse inaction or implausible behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: While characters must remain consistent, their consistency should not mean implausible failure to act (e.g., the Prior who only scolds and never takes reasonable measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters' traits must justify their actions, but authors must still allow believable, necessary actions (calling constables, restraining criminals). Avoid preserving a comic or set mannerism at the cost of credible responses to urgent situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and plausible motivation (avoid afterthoughts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' motives and the reasons for plot choices must be evident and credible (criticises 'after-thought' answers and unexplained conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide antecedent statements or behaviour that account for later choices; do not rely on sudden or weakly justified lines ('all things of fear have lost their power over me' as a poor response to danger). Avoid leaving key decisions unexplained or appearing as contrivances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scenes that exist only for display
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include 'a scene for the sake of a scene'—spectacles or tableaux that do not advance plot, character, or moral purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every scene must serve narrative, thematic, or psychological ends. Anti-pattern: long storm-scenes, set-pieces, or stage-business that add nothing except momentary sensory effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language, diction, and metrical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'solecisms, corrupt diction, and offences against metre,' and words 'chosen without reason' or senseless metaphors and plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain correct idiom, appropriate word choice, and metrical integrity. Refrain from forced or artful archaisms, meaningless grandiloquence, or borrowing lines that do not fit the speaker. Examples of faults: misplaced metaphors, absurd literalizations of metaphors, and unmotivated archaisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetition, tautology, and vague epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of indefinite epithets and mere verbal antitheses weakens style ('repetition... indefinites, seasoned by merely verbal antitheses').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary descriptive language and avoid piling similar epithets or stock phrases that add no fresh meaning. Repetition for its own sake signals laziness of thought and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical stagecraft: audibility, visibility, and believable staging
rubrics_metrics.description: Staging must be sensible and intelligible to the audience (criticises altar spectacle, chorister boys singing on stage, and mute characters moving where 'audience have small chance of hearing a word').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design stage business so actors can be seen and heard, entrance/exit logic makes sense, and on-stage rituals (e.g., sacraments, hymns) are credible within the drama. Avoid conceits that break audience immersion or render dialogue inaudible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective handling of exposition and retrospective narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition should be told 'well and passionately' so as to overcome the difficulty of retrospective narration in first acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate necessary backstory into scenes naturally and compellingly rather than delivering dry summaries. Use dialogue and action to reveal past events in ways that sustain interest and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution and accountability for important plot elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Key plot elements (e.g., the child's fate) must be resolved or meaningfully accounted for rather than left a 'riddle' to the reader/audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close or explain significant story threads; do not introduce important motifs or personages whose outcomes are never addressed. Unresolved major elements undermine the integrity of the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pander to appetite for gratuitous shock or indecency
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid exploiting public taste for 'the grossest and most outrageous stimulants'—shock or indecency offered merely to arouse applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shocking material must have ethical, thematic, or dramatic justification. Do not trade moral seriousness for sensational applause; be cautious of scenes that elicit laughter or plaudits for indecent representation rather than critical reflection.
